target: AG1's claim that animal dissection is ethically acceptable because most specimens are already dead or are unavoidable byproducts, rather than being newly taken from the wild.
objection: AG2 says that this ethical defense is false because approximately 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild. If true, that means dissection causes new harm by reducing local populations and biodiversity, so it is not merely reusing waste animals.

target: AG2's assumption that most dissection specimens come from wild capture rather than existing agricultural or food-industry byproducts.
objection: AG1 argues that a substantial share of classroom dissection specimens are sourced from meat-processing and aquaculture supply chains, such as slaughter byproducts and farmed animals that are already dead when supplied. If specimens are mostly obtained this way, then the claim that dissection mainly depends on wild-caught animals is overstated and likely incorrect.

target: AG1's claim that classroom dissection is primarily a use of already-dead byproducts rather than wild-caught animals.
objection: AG2 restates that the supply is not mainly an already-dead byproduct pipeline and insists that about 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild. On that view, dissection typically causes new wildlife harm instead of just reusing unavoidable waste.

target: AG2's ethical framing that dissection is harmful unless the animals are entirely unavoidable waste, and that any capture or killing makes it objectionable.
objection: AG1 counters that the key issue is incremental harm. If schools obtain specimens that are already dead, such as regulated meat-industry byproducts, then classroom dissection does not require additional capture or killing and therefore substantially reduces the ethical harm AG2 emphasizes.

target: AG1's overall claim that animal dissection provides a worthwhile educational benefit that justifies its use.
objection: AG2 argues that dissection is limited to a one-time, static view of anatomy and lacks repeated, interactive practice. Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the same anatomy and biology content as well or better, without the limitations of dead specimens, so dissection is not uniquely educationally necessary.

target: AG2's claim that alternatives fully match or exceed the learning value of real animal dissection.
objection: AG1 objects that dissection offers distinctive hands-on learning that virtual or synthetic alternatives do not fully replicate, including direct tactile examination of real anatomy and practice with fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, and critical thinking. AG1 also adds that this hands-on experience can inspire science careers and that properly sourced specimens can be already-deceased byproducts, reducing ethical costs.

target: AG1's assumption that dissection can be sourced from already-dead animals so that it does not require additional live capture or killing.
objection: AG2 rejects that sourcing assumption and says that approximately 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild. If that is the common supply route, then dissection usually involves incremental harm to wildlife and biodiversity, undermining the claim that it can be ethically justified as simply using existing dead bodies.

target: AG2's claim that the animal-harm costs outweigh the educational benefits of dissection.
objection: AG1 argues that dissection does teach something alternatives do not fully replicate: real, tactile access to anatomical structures that helps students understand biology and build practical science skills. AG1 also says that if schools use already-deceased byproducts, including fetal pigs from the meat industry, the ethical side of the calculation is substantially reduced.

target: AG1's assumption that alternatives cannot provide students with the same core biology learning outcomes as dissection.
objection: AG2 says that assumption is weak because synthetic models, cadaver-free kits, and computer simulations can show structures realistically, let students label and relate anatomy to function, and allow repeated review. Since AP/NGSS-style biology goals do not require dissection specifically, alternatives can satisfy the learning objectives without dead-animal specimens.
